name: Aaron Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you say here is confidential. Can you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aaron, 58, general foreman for the electricity company's hill district, which is three crews and a lot of rough country. I've been climbing poles since I was nineteen, started as an apprentice under a man called Walt who taught me everything. My wife Ruth keeps our house and does the books for our church, and we've got three grown children. Our boy Caleb followed me into the trade, he's on one of my crews, though I try hard not to play favourites.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the yard on Mill Street at six, coffee from my own flask, and I go through the day's work with the three crew leads face to face. Then I'm out in the truck checking on each crew, signing off work, dealing with landowners who don't want us on their property. I love the brotherhood of it, the way a crew looks out for each other. What wears me out is the new rules from head office every month, written by people who've never seen our hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it. People get carried away with every new gadget. Hard work and good men still keep the lights on, and that won't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means I finish the way I planned. I'd work till 65, see Caleb made a crew lead, and hand over the district in good shape. Then Ruth and I spend more time with the grandchildren and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing at all, keep working. We've got about five months put by, and the house is nearly paid off. I'd keep doing things the way Walt taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. At peace with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has any of this AI stuff reached your district?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head office sent us tablets with some program that's supposed to plan the work. I don't use it, my crew leads do the bare minimum on it. I plan the work on the whiteboard in my office like I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you see your last working years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training up the young apprentices properly, the way I was trained. Nobody learns this job from a screen, they learn it from a man next to them on the pole. That's what I'd want to leave behind.

S0.say: He'd say he knew it all along: people get carried away with every new gadget, and hard work and good men still keep the lights on.
S0.think: It means he finishes as planned: working to 65, seeing his son Caleb made a crew lead and handing over the district in good shape. Then more time with grandchildren and church.
S0.do: Keeps working exactly as before, with about five months of expenses saved and the house nearly paid off. Keeps running the district the way his old mentor Walt taught him.
S0.quote: I plan the work on the whiteboard in my office like I always have.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is a proud, old-school foreman who ignores head office's planning tablets in favour of his whiteboard. His values run through apprenticeship and mentorship, rooted in his own mentor, Walt. His son works on one of his crews, which makes the stakes personal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a good man adapts to his work, but you don't throw away what works. Keep the apprenticeships, keep the crews, use the machines where they help. I'd say that to head office if they asked, which they won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'm probably all right, I'm near the end. But I'd hate to watch the job get turned into a screen job. That's not the trade I came into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what head office actually sent down. I'd let the crew leads handle the tools and I'd keep my whiteboard. I'd keep saving like normal and maybe pay off the last bit of the house early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like something's shifting under my boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's to blame if it goes badly, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big tech companies that sell this stuff to managers who don't understand the work. And the government, for not letting companies run things sensibly, all those rules that make everything slower. Not the workers, never the workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new tools if head office pushed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the bare minimum, honestly. I'm 58, I know my district better than any program. If they forced me, I'd learn enough to sign the forms and not a click more.

S1.say: He'd say a good man adapts to his work but you don't throw away what works: keep the apprenticeships and the crews and use machines where they help. He'd say it to head office if they ever asked.
S1.think: He thinks he's probably fine as he's near the end, but he'd hate to see the job become a screen job. That isn't the trade he came into.
S1.do: Waits to see what head office sends down, leaves the tools to crew leads and keeps his whiteboard. Keeps saving as normal and may pay off the last of the house early.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like something shifting under his boots.
S1.quote: If they forced me, I'd learn enough to sign the forms and not a click more.
S1.fieldNote: His resistance is about identity as much as practicality: he doesn't want the trade turned into screen work. He blames tech sellers and government rules, never the workers. He'd pay off the house early as quiet insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is men in big companies playing God. You don't take a man's work away from him and call it progress. I'd say it from the church steps if I had to, though I'm not one for protests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's my worst nightmare. I'd be 60, five years from where I meant to stop, and my son's job would be going at the same time as mine. Two paycheques in the family gone at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tighten everything straight away: no new truck, no trips, every spare bit into savings. I'd keep working as long as they let me, I wouldn't walk away from my crews. And Ruth and I would talk to the church and to our girls, because family looks after family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be on my knees at night, praying for a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Caleb?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to hold on to his faith and his family, and to take any work that keeps food on the table. I'd tell him that a man who can work with his hands will always find something. Whether that's still true, I honestly don't know any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lean on anyone if things got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, and the church. Our girls are both married, both doing all right. I'd hate it, but if it came to it, we'd lean on them before we'd lean on the government.

S2.say: He'd say this is men in big companies playing God, and that taking a man's work away isn't progress. He'd say it from the church steps if he had to, though he isn't one for protests.
S2.think: It's his worst nightmare: he'd be 60, five years from his planned stop, and his son's job would go at the same time. Two paycheques in the family would disappear at once.
S2.do: Tightens spending immediately, dropping the new truck and trips, and puts every spare bit into savings. Keeps working as long as he's allowed and turns to the church and his married daughters before government help.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying at night for a way through.
S2.quote: Two paycheques in the family gone at once.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline threatens both his job and his son's, which doubles the blow for him. He'd lean on family and church long before government. His belief that working hands always find something cracked in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for a man to get his house in order, and he'd better use it. Don't wait for the government to save you. Get your family ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 when it lands, two years short. That's not the end of the world, I could take the pension early with a cut, but I'd feel cheated out of my last two years. Mostly I'd be thinking about Caleb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the house completely in the next couple of years and keep saving. I'd sit down with Caleb and his wife about their plans, maybe help them pay down their own mortgage. I'd keep working until they tell me to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the fast one, but it doesn't sit easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time make a difference for Caleb?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. Five years is time for him to learn something else if he has to, maybe a trade that still needs people. I'd rather he did it on his own terms than got pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about retiring earlier than 65?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to. A man works while he can, that's how I was raised. But if they offered a fair deal and it meant keeping a young man's job, I might take it so Caleb or one of the apprentices kept theirs.

S3.say: He'd say five years is time for a man to get his house in order, and not to wait for the government to save him. Get your family ready.
S3.think: He'd be 63, two years short, and could take an early pension with a cut, but would feel cheated of his last two years. Mostly he'd be thinking about Caleb.
S3.do: Pays off the house completely in the next couple of years and keeps saving. Sits down with Caleb and his wife about their plans, possibly helping with their mortgage, and keeps working until told to stop.
S3.feel: Anxious, less than with the fast picture, but uneasy all the same.
S3.quote: If they offered a fair deal and it meant keeping a young man's job, I might take it so Caleb or one of the apprentices kept theirs.
S3.fieldNote: Five years softens the money blow but not the sense of loss. His self-reliant streak is strong: get your house in order and don't wait for government. The willingness to step aside so a young man keeps his job was a striking, self-sacrificing note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to stand on their own feet. Learn a trade, look after your family, and don't expect handouts. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm retired by then, 68, God willing. My pension's sorted. What bothers me is Caleb, and the grandchildren, what kind of work there'll be for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and retire at 65, just like planned. I'd spend my last years making sure the apprentices learn the job right. Keep saving, keep the house, nothing different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly for my son and the grandkids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the job properly anyway, because the machines will break and someone has to know how it really works. And to learn how to fix the robots, maybe. Walt would have laughed at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Would you learn the new tools then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'll be gone before it matters, and I'd rather spend my time on the pole and with my family. Let the young ones handle the machines.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to stand on their own feet: learn a trade, look after your family and don't expect handouts.
S4.think: He'll be 68 and retired with his pension sorted. What bothers him is what work there'll be for Caleb and the grandchildren.
S4.do: Carries on and retires at 65 as planned, spending his last years making sure the apprentices learn the job properly. Keeps saving and keeps the house with nothing different.
S4.feel: A bit uneasy, mostly for his son and grandchildren.
S4.quote: And to learn how to fix the robots, maybe. Walt would have laughed at that.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he's personally safe and repeats his self-reliance message. His concern stays with Caleb and the grandchildren. Even with a decade, he won't learn the tools himself, though he can picture apprentices fixing robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, without a doubt, because it takes my job and Caleb's at the same time. What would help is companies keeping the apprenticeships going and giving older men a fair way out, so the young ones can stay on. Not government cheques, I mean real work and a fair deal.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. I'll be honest, when I picture the worst of it, what keeps me steady is that a man's worth isn't his job. It's his family, his word and his God. The job's just how I've served them.

headlineQuote: A man's worth isn't his job. It's his family, his word and his God.
portrait: Aaron Dubois is a 58-year-old general foreman in a hill district who plans the work on a whiteboard, ignores the head-office tablets and wants to work until 65. His son Caleb works on one of his crews, which makes every scenario a family matter. He's calm if AI is hype and uneasy about steady change, but AGI by 2028 alarms him because his and Caleb's paycheques would go at once, and he'd cut spending, save and turn to family and church rather than government. With more time he pays off the house, helps Caleb plan and stays self-reliant, steadied above all by his faith.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would take his job and his son Caleb's at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping apprenticeships going and offering older workers a fair way out so young ones can stay on; real work and a fair deal, not government cheques.
